title: Language core: OOP, equality and hashing
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Interfaces vs abstract classes, records, sealed types, ABC and Protocol, dataclasses, composition over inheritance, and the equals/hashCode contract with its mutable-key traps.
source: Oracle Java Tutorials; JLS; Effective Java (Bloch); Python docs: abc, dataclasses, typing; Baeldung

questions.prompt: In Java, which of these can declare ordinary mutable instance fields (per-object state) that its subclasses inherit?

options.why: Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, so there is no per-object mutable state.
A record can only have the components in its header as instance fields, and they are final; it cannot be extended anyway.
Correct: an abstract class is a normal class that cannot be instantiated, so it may hold state, constructors and concrete methods.
Sealing restricts who may implement it, but it is still an interface with no instance fields.

questions.explanation: Interface vs abstract class is the classic opener. Interfaces (even with default methods, Java 8+) have no instance state and a class may implement many; an abstract class carries state and constructor logic but a class can extend only one.

questions.prompt: Match each construct to what it is for.

right.text: Compact immutable data carrier with generated equals, hashCode and toString
Closed hierarchy: only the classes named in permits may extend it
Structural typing: any class with the right methods satisfies it for the type checker
Nominal base class: instantiating a subclass that skips an abstract method raises TypeError

questions.explanation: Records and dataclasses remove boilerplate, sealed types give exhaustive switches, Protocol is the typed form of duck typing, and ABC enforces a contract by inheritance.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Inheritance couples a subclass to its superclass more tightly than composition couples a wrapper to a collaborator.
questions.reason: A subclass can depend on implementation details of the superclass, such as which overridable methods call each other.

whys.a: Correct: the fragile base class problem is exactly this hidden dependence, which a wrapper that only uses the public API avoids.
whys.b: R is not merely true, it is the reason A holds.
whys.c: R is true: self-use of overridable methods is a documented source of bugs.
whys.d: A is true; Effective Java item 18 says to favour composition over inheritance.

questions.explanation: Effective Java: design for inheritance or prohibit it. Composition plus delegation (forwarding class) keeps the dependency to the public contract.

questions.prompt: A subclass of HashSet<String> counts additions: add(e) does count++ then super.add(e); addAll(c) does count += c.size() then super.addAll(c). After one call addAll(List.of("a","b","c")) on a new instance, what is count?
questions.explanation: HashSet.addAll (inherited from AbstractCollection) calls the overridden add for every element, so each element is counted twice: 3 + 3 = 6. This is the textbook case for composition over inheritance. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about Python abstract base classes.
questions.text: A class that inherits from abc.ABC and leaves a method decorated with @{1} unimplemented raises {2} as soon as you try to instantiate it.
questions.explanation: The check happens at instantiation, not at class definition. NotImplementedError is what a plain base-class method raises by convention when you do not use ABC.

questions.prompt: Write a Python frozen dataclass named Point with float fields x and y so that instances are immutable and hashable.
questions.explanation: frozen=True makes assignment raise FrozenInstanceError and, together with the default eq=True, generates __hash__ from the fields. A NamedTuple would also work but is not what the question asks.

questions.prompt: A class must explicitly inherit from a typing.Protocol to satisfy it for a static type checker such as mypy.

options.why: Protocols are structural: the base class is not required.
Correct: mypy checks the method signatures, so no inheritance is needed (only @runtime_checkable matters for isinstance).

questions.explanation: That is the difference between nominal (ABC) and structural (Protocol) typing, the Python counterpart of Go-style interfaces.

questions.prompt: Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;  How many of the four expressions a == b, c == d, c.equals(d), a.equals(b) evaluate to true?
questions.explanation: Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf, which caches -128..127, so a == b is true but c == d compares two distinct objects and is false. Both equals calls are true: 3 true. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Write a final class Point { private final int x, y; } with equals(Object) and hashCode() that follow the contract (value equality on x and y).

checks.label: checks the type with instanceof or getClass

questions.explanation: A record Point(int x, int y) generates all of this. getClass() versus instanceof is a debate: instanceof is fine for a final class. Other correct spellings (31 * x + y) also pass.

options.why: The entry was filed under the hash of [1]; after the mutation the hash is different, so the lookup goes to another bucket.
Correct: the entry is still in the map (size 1) but is unreachable by either the mutated key or an equal new list.
containsKey would only be true if the entry were found; it sits in the bucket of the old hash.
Mutating a key never removes the entry, and get(k) cannot succeed here.

questions.explanation: Never use a mutable object as a HashMap key (or HashSet element) if its hashCode depends on mutable state. The entry becomes a leak: present but unfindable. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: If a class overrides equals() but not hashCode(), two equal objects can both end up in the same HashSet.
questions.reason: The hashCode() contract requires a different hash value for every pair of unequal objects.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false: the contract only demands equal objects have equal hashes.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because the default identity hashCode usually sends equal objects to different buckets; R is false (collisions between unequal objects are allowed).
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may share a hash code (it only affects performance).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Python dataclass declared with @dataclass(frozen=True) is unhashable.
questions.reason: A dataclass with eq=True and frozen=False gets __hash__ set to None.

whys.a: A is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: frozen=True with eq=True generates __hash__ from the fields, so A is false; R is true (the default mutable dataclass is unhashable).

questions.explanation: eq=True, frozen=False sets __hash__ to None; eq=True, frozen=True generates a field-based __hash__; unsafe_hash=True forces one.

questions.prompt: Select all that are safe to use as HashMap keys (value-based equality, hash stable over time).

options.why: Immutable, value-based equals, and the hash is cached.

options.text: A record Pair(String name, int age)
options.why: Records get value-based equals/hashCode from immutable components.

options.text: An ArrayList you keep adding to
options.why: Its hashCode changes with its contents, so the entry gets lost.

options.text: A StringBuilder used as the key
options.why: It does not override equals/hashCode, so lookups only work by identity, and its contents are mutable.

questions.explanation: Immutable value types make good keys. Identity-hashed mutable objects only match themselves, and content-hashed mutable ones break when they change.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java record is implicitly final.
questions.reason: The equals method of a record compares all of its components.

whys.a: Both are true, but the equality semantics have nothing to do with why records cannot be extended.
whys.b: Correct: records are final (they cannot be subclassed), and generated equals compares components, but one does not explain the other.
whys.d: A is true: record classes are implicitly final.

questions.explanation: Records are shallowly immutable data carriers: final class, final fields, accessors, and component-based equals/hashCode/toString.
